author: Tertullian
occasion: Tertullian writes to the proconsul Scapula during a time of persecution of Christians in Africa, urging him to stop punishing Christians and warning him of divine judgment.
argument: Tertullian argues that Christians do not fear persecution and that their suffering is part of their commitment to God. He insists that Christians are loyal subjects who pray for the emperor's safety, and that they are innocent of the crimes alleged against them. He warns that persecuting Christians brings divine punishment, citing examples of officials who suffered for their cruelty. He urges Scapula to follow the example of governors who dealt leniently with Christians, and concludes by warning that persecution only strengthens the church.

outline.move: Tertullian explains that Christians do not fear suffering and writes not for their own sake but out of love for their enemies, including Scapula.
He defends Christian worship of one God, argues that religion cannot be forced, and insists that Christians are loyal to the emperor and pray for his safety.
He warns that no city escapes punishment for shedding Christian blood, citing portents and the fates of officials who persecuted Christians.
He urges Scapula to follow the example of governors who treated Christians leniently, and lists the good deeds and innocence of Christians.
He warns that persecution only strengthens the church, and urges Scapula to spare himself, Carthage, and the province.

cast.name: Scapula
cast.who: The proconsul of Africa to whom Tertullian addresses this letter.

cast.name: Hilarianus
cast.who: A governor under whom crowds cried out against Christian burial grounds; the crop failure that followed is presented as divine punishment on the crowd or city, not specifically on Hilarianus himself.

cast.name: Vigellius Saturninus
cast.who: The first governor to use the sword against Christians in Africa; he lost his eyesight.

cast.name: Claudius Lucius Herminianus
cast.who: A governor in Cappadocia who persecuted Christians and died of plague, nearly becoming a Christian himself.

cast.name: Caecilius Capella
cast.who: A man who at his death cried out, 'Christians, rejoice!'; the text does not explicitly identify him as a governor.

cast.name: Mavilus of Hadrumetum
cast.who: A Christian condemned to the beasts by Scapula.

cast.name: Cincius Severus
cast.who: A governor at Thysdrus who gave Christians a way to answer so they could be released.

cast.name: Vespronius Candidus
cast.who: A governor who released a Christian under the pretext that he was a troublemaker, to satisfy his fellow citizens.

cast.name: Asper
cast.who: A governor who lightly punished a Christian and did not force him to sacrifice.

cast.name: Pudens
cast.who: A governor who dismissed a Christian's case after understanding it from the indictment, tore up the indictment, and refused to hear the man without an accuser, citing the mandate.

cast.name: Septimius Severus
cast.who: The emperor, father of Antoninus (Caracalla); he protected Christians and honored them.

cast.name: Proculus
cast.who: A Christian nicknamed Torpacion, procurator of Euhodia, who had cured Severus with oil and lived in his palace.

cast.name: Marcus Aurelius
cast.who: Emperor whose army was saved by rain through the prayers of Christian soldiers.

cast.name: Arrius Antoninus
cast.who: A governor in Asia who was overwhelmed when all the Christians of a city offered themselves for martyrdom.

key_terms.sense: The Christian faith or way of life, as viewed by outsiders and adopted by Tertullian.
The pagan gods, whom Christians regard as evil spirits.
The charge of impiety or temple-robbing brought against Christians.
The majesty or sovereign dignity of the emperor, violation of which was treason.
The Christian teaching and way of life that commands love of enemies and patient endurance.
The endurance and forbearance Christians show under persecution.
The public acknowledgment of being a Christian, which led to condemnation.
The moral blamelessness of Christians, contrasted with the crimes alleged against them.
The divine wrath that Tertullian warns will fall on persecutors.
Portents and omens that warn of impending divine judgment.
The act of offering sacrifice to the pagan gods, which Christians refuse.
The written indictment or charge against a Christian brought before a governor.
Torture used to force Christians to deny their faith.
A Roman provincial governor with judicial authority over Christians.
Wild beasts to which condemned Christians were thrown in the arena.

scripture: Tertullian does not quote Scripture directly in this work, but he refers to Christian teaching about loving enemies and praying for persecutors (cf. Matthew 5:44). Biblical names and Psalm numbering are not relevant here.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is uncertain; c. 212 is a common estimate based on Scapula's proconsulship.
The reading of the name 'By(??)mtinor' in section 3 is uncertain; it may refer to Byzantium or another place.
The reading of 'pala(??)' in section 4 is uncertain; it may be 'palam' (openly) or another word.
The reading of 'Anto(??)s' in section 4 is uncertain; it likely refers to Antoninus (Caracalla).
The reading of 'Ievis nomine' in section 4 is uncertain; it may be a reference to the name of Jesus or a textual corruption.
The exact identity of 'the governor of Legion' and 'the governor of Mauretania' in section 4 is uncertain.
The reading 'Gemanica' in section 4 is likely a corruption for 'Germanica' (German campaign).

_unresolved_facts.claim: Hilarianus: 'A governor under whom crowds cried out against Christian burial grounds; the crop failure that followed is presented as divine punishment on the crowd or city, not specifically on Hilarianus himself.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: sicut et sub Hilariano praeside, cum de areis sepulturarum nostrarum adclamassent: Areae non sint! areae ipsorum non fuerunt! Messes enim suas non egerunt.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text presents the crop failure as divine punishment specifically on those who cried out (the crowd), not on Hilarianus himself. However, the brief's phrasing 'not specifically on Hilarianus himself' is accurate but understates that the text explicitly says 'areae ipsorum non fuerunt' (their lands did not exist) and 'Messes enim suas non egerunt' (for they did not reap their harvests), directing punishment at the crowd, not the governor.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The crowd under Hilarianus: 'Direct quotation in Latin', sections: ['3']
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: cum de areis sepulturarum nostrarum adclamassent: Areae non sint!
_unresolved_facts.fix: The brief incorrectly identifies 'Areae non sint!' as a direct quotation from the crowd. The actual quotation from the crowd is 'Areae non sint!' (Let there be no lands/areas!). However, Tertullian's response 'areae ipsorum non fuerunt!' (their lands did not exist!) is his own commentary, not the crowd's words. The brief should clarify that 'Areae non sint!' is the crowd's cry, and the rest is Tertullian's ironic retort.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The crowd at Carthage: 'Direct quotation in Latin', sections: ['4']
_unresolved_facts.fix: There is no direct quotation from a crowd at Carthage in section 4. The brief appears to be inventing this voice. The acclamations mentioned are: the crowd in section 3 under Hilarianus ('Areae non sint!'), and in section 4 'Tunc et populus adclamans duo deorum, qui solus potens, in Ievis nomine deo nostre testimonium reddidit' — but this is a crowd witnessing rain, not at Carthage specifically, and the quotation is not clearly demarcated as direct speech.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Pudens: 'A governor who dismissed a Christian's case after understanding it from the indictment, tore up the indictment, and refused to hear the man without an accuser, citing the mandate.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Pudens etiam missum ad se Christianum in elogio concussione eius intellecta dimisit, scisso eodem elogio, aine accusatore negans se auditurum hominem secundum mandatum.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text says 'sine accusatore' (without an accuser), not 'aine accusatore' (which appears to be a typo in the source text). More importantly, the brief says 'citing the mandate' but the Latin says 'secundum mandatum' (according to the mandate). The brief's 'citing' is acceptable, but the source text has a clear reading issue: 'aine' should be 'sine'. The brief should note the textual issue.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Proculus: 'A Christian nicknamed Torpacion, procurator of Euhodia, who had cured Severus with oil and lived in his palace.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Proculum Christianum, qui Torpacion cognominabatur, Euhodiae procuratorem, qui eum par oleum aliquando curaverat
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text says 'par oleum' (a small amount of oil), not that he cured Severus 'with oil' generally. More importantly, the text says Severus 'requisivit et in palatio suo habuit usque ad mortem eius' (sought him out and had him in his palace until [Proculus's?] death). The brief's 'lived in his palace' overstates the arrangement; 'habuit' suggests he kept/retained him there, but 'usque ad mortem eius' is ambiguous — whose death? Likely Proculus's, but the brief should be more cautious.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Marcus Aurelius: 'Emperor whose army was saved by rain through the prayers of Christian soldiers.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Marcus quoque Aurelius in Gemanica expeditione Christianorum militum orationibus ad deum fectis imbres in siti illa impetrarit
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text says 'in siti illa' (in that thirst/drought), not that the army was 'saved'. The rain was obtained 'in that thirst' — the brief overstates by saying 'saved'. Also 'Gemanica' is a textual corruption for 'Germanica' as noted in uncertain, but the brief doesn't flag this in the cast entry.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Caecilius Capella: 'Direct quotation in Latin', sections: ['3']
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Caecilius Capella in illo exitu By(??)mtinor, Christiani gaudete (??) exclamavit.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text is highly corrupt here: 'By(??)mtinor, Christiani gaudete (??)'. The brief reconstructs this as a direct quotation 'Christians, rejoice!' but the source has lacunae and unclear text. The brief should flag this as uncertain rather than presenting it as a clear direct quotation.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Mavilus of Hadrumetum: 'A Christian condemned to the beasts by Scapula.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Tibi quoque optamus admonitionem solam fuisse, quod cum Adrumeticum Mavilum ad bestias damnasses
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text confirms Mavilus was condemned to the beasts by Scapula, but the brief's name 'Mavilus of Hadrumetum' adds 'of Hadrumetum' which is not in the source. The source says 'Adrumeticum Mavilum' — 'Adrumeticum' is an adjective meaning 'of Hadrumetum/Adrumetum', describing Mavilus. The brief's formulation is acceptable but should note that 'Adrumeticum' is the source form, not 'Mavilus of Hadrumetum'.
The source has 'Adrumeticum' (adjectival form), not 'Adrumetum'. The brief should include 'Adrumetum/Adrumeticum' or note the adjectival form in the source.
